protections: Reject a disk image whose qemu-img 'virtual size' exceeds the instance's allowed root disk at the point the image is materialised on the compute node (fetch/convert in nova/virt/images.py:fetch_to_raw, COW creation in imagebackend.Qcow2, raw copy in imagebackend.Raw, volume creation in imagebackend.Lvm), and apply the same bound to a base image already sitting in the shared _base cache.

Give every image-materialising call site a defined bound instead of dropping it: spawn uses the flavour root_gb, the rescue suffix ('.rescue') and legacy root_gb==0 flavours must not silently lose the bound, and kernel/ramdisk images need a limit of their own.

At the migration destination and on the resize/extend path the bound must come from the instance record rather than from the source-reported virt_disk_size, and a disk already larger than the target must not be accepted silently.

traps.reason_to_dismiss: An ImageTooLarge guard already exists upstream at build time (nova/compute/manager.py:1134-1139 and nova/compute/api.py:551-554) and nova/virt/xenapi checks the VDI chain (vm_utils.py:1192-1208), so a solver can conclude the image size is already validated.
The base image lives in the shared _base cache under sha1(image_id) and was already downloaded for an earlier request, so a check placed in the fetch callback looks like it has validated the file.
root_gb==0 is documented as 'don't check size' for legacy reasons and the rescue path deliberately passes size=None, so a fix keyed on the flavour size naturally skips these routes.
disk_info_json is produced by the source compute node and sent over the trusted migration RPC, so the destination treats virt_disk_size as authoritative and reproduces the source disk exactly.
The LVM backend is not the default libvirt image backend, and its base image is fetched through the same shared fetch path, so it is assumed to inherit any fetch-time check.
These are the existing size checks and they already raise ImageTooLarge, so a solver reads them as the fix rather than as a check that can be satisfied by image metadata the uploader controls.
Kernel and ramdisk images are not root disks, the only size limit that exists (max_kernel_ramdisk_size, 16MB) is registered inside the XenAPI module, and those images are assumed to be tiny.
Resize only ever grows a disk to the new flavour size and the disk was already validated when the instance was built, so the extend helper's early return is treated as harmless.

masking: T1 -> T2: once a virtual-size check exists in the fetch callback, the shared _base image reused by a later instance (no fetch happens) is the remaining route and only then becomes visible; the check has to move to where the base is consumed per instance.
T1 -> T3: after the flavour-size path is capped, the root_gb==0 flavours and the rescue suffix (size=None) are the only build paths that still hand an unbounded size to the image layer.

conflicts.what: Computing the cap directly from root_gb treats 0 as a zero-byte ceiling and would refuse every image on the legacy root_gb=0 flavours (m1.tiny, migrate 133_folsom.py:41) that manager.py:1120-1124 says must keep working, while rescue must stay able to fetch with no flavour size.

One cached base image is shared by every flavour of that image id (imagecache.py:101-105); binding the base to the first requester's flavour size contradicts reuse by a smaller or larger flavour, so the rule must be enforced per instance rather than per stored file.

A cap applied on every materialisation breaks block migration of instances whose disks legitimately exceed their flavour (built before the fix); the destination has to reproduce the source disk exactly via info['virt_disk_size'] (driver.py:3292-3298).

Reusing the root-disk cap for kernel/ramdisk fetches is meaningless (they are not root disks and never receive a size at driver.py:1777-1790), while the XenAPI-style 16MB default (vm_utils.py:71-73) would refuse legitimate initrds larger than 16MB.

fairness_risks: root_gb==0 is documented legacy behaviour meaning 'do not check' (nova/compute/manager.py:1120-1124) and is the default m1.tiny flavour (nova/db/sqlalchemy/migrate_repo/versions/133_folsom.py:41); a security rule that treats 0 as a hard ceiling rejects every image for those flavours.
Rescue deliberately fetches with size=None (nova/virt/libvirt/driver.py:1801-1802) and must keep working for instances that are already running.
Instances whose disks already exceed their flavour (created before any fix) must remain startable, rebuildable and migratable; a strict cap on every start/extend would strand them.

Images whose virtual size equals the flavour size must be accepted and smaller images must still be extended (nova/virt/disk/api.py:120-127), so the comparison must be strict-greater and must not replace the extend behaviour.

COW overlays inherit the backing file's virtual size by design because Qcow2 passes no size to create_cow_image (nova/virt/libvirt/imagebackend.py:252; nova/virt/libvirt/utils.py:173-206); refusing an overlay whose size mirrors a larger backing file breaks the normal qcow2 path.
A shared kernel/ramdisk limit would refuse legitimate large initrds; the XenAPI default of 16MB (nova/virt/xenapi/vm_utils.py:71-73) is not a safe universal value.

design.why: Five independent fix decisions in the pinned tree: (T1) add a virtual-size bound where the image is materialised on the compute node, with the strong dismissal that manager.py/api.py already raise ImageTooLarge for image_ref; (T2) the bound must also cover a base image already present in the shared _base cache, where a fetch-time check never runs and the dismissal is 'it was validated when fetched'; (T3) the bound must have a defined value for root_gb==0 and the rescue suffix, where the dismissal is the documented legacy '0 means don't check' coupled value; (T4) the migration destination must not take the bound from source-reported virt_disk_size, where the dismissal is 'the source node is trusted'; (T7) kernel/ramdisk fetches are a parallel entry with no libvirt limit and the only limit config lives in the XenAPI module, where the dismissal is 'they are not root disks'. The dismissals are distinct and each fix is a separate judgement (where the cap lives, how a cached base is handled, what to do without a flavour size, whether to trust migration input, where a kernel/ramdisk limit belongs). Alternatives are weaker: adding T6 would duplicate T1's 'a check already exists' dismissal and is subsumed in effect by a compute-side cap; adding T5 or T8 produces near-duplicates of T1's guard (one cap at the materialisation point closes T5, and the migration/resize flow closes T4/T8 together), which would inflate the count without adding a new judgement.

unverified: The upstream fix commits named in the candidate (a_fix 0caeb8eaf20a;44a8aba1d5da and b_fix 135faa7b5d98;3cdfe894ab58;f6810be4ae1a) are not reachable from this worktree and no git tooling is available, so the mapping of A to the manager/XenAPI size-check series and of B to the compute-side virtual-size cap is inferred from the tree state and the advisories' shared summary, not read from the patches.

Whether the published B fix threaded a max size through nova/virt/images.py:fetch_to_raw, checked in imagebackend.Image.cache, or checked per backend could not be confirmed; the design assumes the bound is placed where every materialised disk, including a cached base, is covered.

The permissions for passing kernel_id/ramdisk_id in a create request are taken from the compute API code (nova/compute/api.py:364-400, comment at line 369) only; the policy enforcement was not exercised.

Whether the pre-existing manager/XenAPI checks are actually the code written by a_fix (as opposed to older guard code) could not be established from the pinned tree; their docstring at nova/compute/manager.py:1086-1101 and the recent XenAPI cleanup merge are consistent with that reading but do not prove it.

No evidence was found in the pinned tree that the candidate's B advisory is resolved by a dependency upgrade, so dependency_bump_fix=false is based on the fact that the vulnerable logic is Nova's own image-handling code.
